# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like. Everyone files into a conference room—or these days, joins a video call—and after some discussion, the group converges on a shared conclusion. Nods all around. Someone volunteers to write up the summary. The meeting ends early, and everyone leaves feeling productive. Agreement, in this picture, is the currency of progress. If people leave the room still arguing, something has gone wrong.

This picture is comforting, but it is often wrong. In many cases, a meeting that ends in easy agreement is a meeting that has failed in a subtler and more dangerous way. Agreement can conceal uncertainty. It can paper over the fact that different people, sitting around the same table and using the same words, are actually imagining very different things. The most valuable thing a group can produce is not a warm sense of unity but a precise map of what it doesn't yet know—and a plan for finding out.
